OIG made **148 recommendations** in Healthcare Facility Inspection reports published in 2026, and **80 of them (about 54%) are still open**.

This data is current as of **November 4, 2026**, so it doesn't include anything OIG publishes later in the year.

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Reports published | 61 |
| Recommendations made | 148 |
| **Still open** | **80** |
| Closed, implemented | 68 |
| Closed, not implemented | 0 |

**What affects these numbers:**
- **Report count:** The 61 reports can include some that made no recommendations.
- **Recently closed recommendations:** For half or more of the 68 closed recommendations, the closure date is the day the report was published. The facility probably fixed the problem during the inspection, before the report came out. So the typical "0 days to close" doesn't show how long fixes usually take.
- **Why so many are open:** Most of these reports came out within the past year. It's normal for many recent recommendations to still be open because facilities are still carrying out their fixes. This doesn't necessarily mean anything has stalled.
- **Matching OIG's website:** OIG's own dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all report types, and this data shows 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the 19-item gap comes from blank rows on OIG's pages. So the 2026 open count should match what OIG lists.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. The underlying data is OIG's recommendations listing at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all. If it would help, I can break the 80 open recommendations down by facility, VISN or topic, or list the specific reports.

OIG issued the most recommendations in **2015: 1,914**, across 396 reports. That's the most in any year in the data.

**The busiest years:**

| Year | Recommendations | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| **2015** | **1,914** | 396 |
| 2014 | 1,670 | 217 |
| 2013 | 1,394 | 209 |
| 2020 | 1,211 | 150 |
| 2017 | 1,152 | 216 |

Since 2016, the yearly count has stayed between about 600 and 1,200. The low was 602 in 2022. In 2026 (through November 4), OIG has issued 631 so far.

**Things to keep in mind:**
- **Early years aren't really covered.** Reports go back to 1996, but almost none of the reports from before 2012 have recommendations attached in this data. That's probably a gap in OIG's recommendation tracking for older reports, not proof that OIG made no recommendations back then. So 2015 is the peak only within the years the data actually covers.
- **A drop in the count can mean different things.** The fall after 2015 could mean facilities improved. It could also mean OIG changed its inspection methods, published fewer reports, or shifted its focus. These numbers can't tell those apart.
- **The total is slightly incomplete.** This data has 15,649 recommendations, while OIG's dashboard shows 15,778, a difference of 129. A row-by-row check confirmed that every recommendation OIG lists appears here. The ranking wouldn't change, but a few years' counts could be a little low.

The data is current as of November 4, 2026 and isn't stale. Because these are totals across many reports, no single report is the source. They come from the VA OIG recommendations page (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all).

run.answer:
No. By this measure, suicide is not a growing theme. Mentions of suicide in recommendations dropped sharply from 2024 to 2025, but the drop mostly reflects a change in how OIG runs inspections, not clear evidence of less concern or fewer problems.

**The counts** (data as of 2026-11-04, not stale):

| Year | Reports with a recommendation mentioning suicide | Those recommendations | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 10 | 17 | 117 | ~9% |
| 2023 | 32 | 77 | 142 | ~23% |
| **2024** | **56** | **98** | 155 | **~36%** |
| **2025** | **11** | **19** | 132 | **~8%** |

Searching for "suicidal" instead gave exactly the same numbers, so the search probably catches different forms of the word. These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source.

**Why the 2025 drop mostly reflects a program change:**
- **2024:** 55 of the 98 recommendations came from the Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program (CHIP). Its standard review areas regularly produced suicide-related recommendations. The rest came from hotline inspections (18), Vet Center inspections (15), national reviews (8) and mental health inspections (2).
- **2025:** CHIP produced none. Its replacement, the Healthcare Facility Inspection program, made 190 recommendations across 2024–2025, and none of them used the word suicide. The 19 that did came from mental health inspections (9), Vet Center inspections (5), national reviews (3) and hotline inspections (2).

**What the counts can show:**
- How often recommendation text uses the word suicide, by year and by type of inspection.
- That the 2023–2024 rise and the 2025 fall line up with CHIP's last years and its replacement.
- The status of those recommendations. All 98 from 2024 are closed as implemented. Of the 19 from 2025, 6 are still open and 13 are closed as implemented.

**What the counts cannot show:**
- **Whether suicide prevention got better or worse.** OIG's own caveat applies: a falling count can mean the problem improved, or that inspection methods, report volume or OIG's focus changed. Here the program change is the most visible cause, but the counts can't tell those explanations apart.
- **How much OIG actually focuses on the topic.** Searching recommendation wording misses work that is described in other terms, like safety planning, risk screening, lethal means or high-risk flags. It also misses cases where OIG looked at suicide prevention and found nothing to recommend. A falling count could even partly mean fewer problems were found.
- **How serious the findings were.** A routine paperwork gap and a finding tied to a patient death each count as one.
- **A settled 2025 figure.** Some 2025 reports may still be added to the data, and the open recommendations will keep changing status.
- **A tidy subject tag.** OIG labeled only about a quarter of its reports with topics like "Suicide Prevention," so I searched the wording instead. Topic-based counts would be incomplete.

If you want a fairer picture of the trend, I could repeat the count using related terms, or count only the mental health inspection program.

**The median Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA) recommendation takes 179 days to close, or about 6 months.** The data is current as of **2026-11-04** and is not stale.

**What 179 days measures**
- It's the time from the day the OIG report was published to the day OIG marked the recommendation closed on its website.
- It only includes **closed** VBA recommendations that have a closure date: 914 of the 923 closed ones. Open recommendations are left out. About 6% of closed recommendations across all of OIG, mostly from 2013–2016, show no closure date.
- The closure date seems to record when OIG reviewed VBA's evidence and accepted it, not when VBA finished the work. That review can come months later, so the figure measures how long OIG takes to sign off, which may be longer than the fix itself.
- It doesn't show whether VBA met its own target dates. Those dates are VBA's estimates, and this data can't tell whether they were met.
- 110 recommendations were closed the day their report came out, presumably because they were fixed before publication. They count as 0 days and pull the median down a little.

**Spread and status of all 966 VBA recommendations**

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Middle half closed between | 134 and 312.5 days |
| Closed | 923 (897 implemented, 26 not implemented, a 2.8% not-implemented rate) |
| Still open | 43 (median age 161 days; 17 open over a year; oldest 1,567 days) |

**What's included:** I counted every recommendation that names VBA as a responsible office, including ones shared with another office. A recommendation that names two offices counts for both. That's why a few shared items also show up under other offices (11 with Information and Technology and 5 with the Veterans Health Administration). Their medians come from very small groups and say little about VBA.

**Source:** These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. The data comes from VA OIG's public recommendations listing (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all), as of 2026-11-04.

**Overall breakdown**
- 66 recommendations from 19 OIG reports. 11 of those reports, mostly from 2004–2016, have no recommendations recorded.
- **4 open**
- 62 closed as implemented
- 0 closed as not implemented

A separate count by year came out the same: 23 recommendations from 2014 reports, 10 from 2017, 7 from 2019, 12 from 2022, 11 from 2023, 1 from 2024 and 2 from 2026.

**The 4 open recommendations and their reports**

1. **Report 25-00193-155**, *Healthcare Facility Inspection of the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas* (published 16 July 2026). This is the most recent inspection, on site 14–16 January 2025. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system
   - **Rec 1 (environment of care):** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." The facility agreed and set a target date of 29 January 2027. Its plan centers on cleaning by environmental services staff, documented on restroom cleaning logs.
   - **Rec 2 (primary care):** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." The facility agreed and set a target date of 31 December 2026. It reports zero unresolved secondary screenings older than 30 days on its dashboard and says it is formalizing a standard operating procedure.

2. **Report 23-01179-204**, *Inspection of Information Security at the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas* (published 27 September 2023). https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare
   - **Rec 5:** "Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center."
   - **Rec 7:** "Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center."
   - Both are assigned to VA's Office of Information and Technology and have been open for over 3 years. The other 6 recommendations in this report are closed. No facility response was pulled out of this report. That doesn't mean the facility didn't respond or that anything is overdue, because responses are mostly extracted from healthcare inspection reports.

**Things to keep in mind**
- **How reports are matched to El Paso:** Most reports are linked by station number. Some, including the information security inspection above and the 2022 Financial Efficiency Review (12 recommendations, all closed), are linked because the report title names the facility.
- **Small differences from OIG's own totals:** Across all facilities, OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations and this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages, so the El Paso numbers shouldn't be affected.
- **Comparing years:** If you compare years, a change in the number of recommendations could mean conditions changed. It could also reflect changes in OIG's inspection programs, how many reports it published, or where it focused.

OIG made **two recommendations** in report **25-00193-155**, *Healthcare Facility Inspection of the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas*, published July 16, 2026.

1. **Environment of care:** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment."
2. **Primary care:** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days."

**Recommendation 1 (clean and safe environment)**
- **Did the facility agree?** Yes, it concurred.
- **Target date:** January 29, 2027.
- **Status:** Still open as of the data date. It has no closure date.
- **What the facility said it would do:**
  - Cleaning staff clean all areas at least once a day. Restroom cleaning logs are posted where the public can see them.
  - One cleaning technician checks high-traffic public restrooms throughout each business day.
  - 24 standard procedures for cleaning and disinfection are now in place, and cleaning staff were trained on them on June 2, 2026.
  - The cleaning services chief checks cleanliness every day, and the Associate Director checks it during weekly safety rounds.
  - At an all-staff town hall on June 2, 2026, all employees were told their role in keeping the facility clean and safe.

One thing to know about the source: the stored response for this recommendation also contains text that appears to come from the report itself. OIG says it made no recommendation for those because the facility had already fixed them. A damaged restroom floor is also described, but that part of the text cuts off. Check page 12 of the PDF for the exact wording of the facility's response.

**The most common recurring finding is about how test results get communicated, and El Paso is not in that group.** The data is current as of November 4, 2026, and is not stale.

**The most common finding**

The cluster that shows up in the most current-program inspection reports asks the **Chief of Staff and the Associate Director for Patient Care Services to write workflows showing how each team member helps communicate test results.** This is required by VHA Directive 1088(1), *Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients*.

- **How common:** it appears in **21 of 112 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports (about 19%)**, covering 26 recommendations. All of them were cited in 2026.
- **Status:** 17 of the 26 are still open.
- **Time to close:** the median is 0 days, but that number isn't meaningful. Only 9 recommendations have closure data, and some closed the day their report came out, which pulls the median to 0. Too few have closed to know how long these usually take.
- **A related cluster:** a second, similarly worded cluster about test-result policy and patient notification appears in 12 more reports. Of those with closure data, half closed in about 229 to 320 days (median 256). One topic can be split across several clusters, so 21 undercounts how often test-result communication comes up overall. I can't simply add 21 and 12, because the two clusters may share reports.

These clusters are built by grouping recommendations with similar wording. That suggests a shared problem, but it doesn't prove a common cause.

**El Paso (station 756)**

El Paso's latest Healthcare Facility Inspection is report **25-00193-155** (on site January 14–16, 2025; published July 16, 2026): https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system

It made only two recommendations, and neither is about test-result communication. Both are still open:
1. **"Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment"** (target date January 29, 2027). This one also recurs across facilities. It falls in a separate clean-environment cluster (#270), not one of the five most common, though the top list includes similar clean-environment clusters in 11 and 9 reports.
2. **"The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days"** (target date December 31, 2026). This doesn't match any recurring cluster.

The data shows **no repeat findings** for El Paso. A repeat would mean the same standard recommendation was cited again in a later report. That would show the issue came up again, not that nothing was done in between.

Even though El Paso wasn't cited for test-result workflows, it's the finding OIG cites most under this program. If you're preparing for the next inspection, it's worth checking against Directive 1088. My estimate for the next one is around **January 2028**: three years after the last inspection ended, based on the program's roughly three-year cycle. OIG doesn't publish a schedule.

**1. Atlanta VA Medical Center, Decatur, Georgia — Report 13-03653-91** (published March 12, 2014)
- **Recommendation:** Strengthen processes so medication carts are secured at all times, and monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to:**
  - Nursing staff would keep carts secured at all times.
  - Some carts had locks that didn't work. Those would be repaired or replaced. Six new carts had arrived, 26 more were on order, and buying the rest was underway.
  - Until then, carts would stay in a locked medication room whenever they weren't in use.

**2. Battle Creek VA Medical Center, Battle Creek, Michigan — Report 15-00606-495** (published August 31, 2015)
- **Recommendation:** Staff must secure medication carts when not in use, and managers must monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to:**
  - Inpatient mental health medication nurses would check that every drawer is locked each time the cart is opened.
  - Nurse managers would do random weekly checks of every cart until compliance stayed at 100% for 90 days.

# El Paso inspection prep (Station 756, VISN 17)

This comes from OIG's public records as of **4 November 2026**, which is current. OIG doesn't rate facilities, and this doesn't either.

## 1. When the next inspection might happen (an estimate only)
- **Your last inspection:** Healthcare Facility Inspection, report **25-00193-155**. The site visit ended 16 January 2025 and the report was published 16 July 2026. [Report](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system)
- **Rough estimate for the next one: around January 2028.** OIG publishes no schedule. This is just your last site visit plus the program's stated cycle of about three years, so treat it as a planning guess, not a date.

## 2. Your own open items (4 of 66 recommendations across 19 reports)
Inspectors usually check whether earlier findings were actually fixed, so these come first.

| Recommendation | Report | Your target date | Status of your plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rec 1: Keep the environment clean and safe** (Environment of Care) | 25-00193-155 | 31 Jan 2027 | 24 cleaning procedures, staff training (2 June 2026), restroom cleaning logs, a technician checking high-traffic restrooms, daily checks by the Environmental Management chief, weekly rounds by the Associate Director |
| **Rec 2: Complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days** (Primary Care) | 25-00193-155 | 31 Dec 2026 | Zero screenings over 30 days as of June 2026. Monthly reports to the Clinical Executive Council started June 2026. **The written procedure was still being drafted.** Your goal is six months in a row at zero. |
| **Rec 5: Working, monitored video surveillance in the data center** | 23-01179-204 (Information Security) [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare) | none in the data | Open since September 2023 |
| **Rec 7: Water detection sensors in the data center** | 23-01179-204 | none in the data | Open since September 2023 |

**What to do:**
- **Toxic exposure screening:** Finish and approve the written procedure. Keep the monthly council minutes showing zero overdue screenings, since your six months of data run through about November 2026. That's the evidence you'll need to ask OIG to close it.
- **Cleaning:** Keep the audit results, not just the plans. That means the logs, the weekly round results and the training records.
- **Data center items:** These are VA's IT office's to fix, but they're the oldest open items and nothing in the record shows a plan. Ask your IT office for a status update and a target date.

No repeat findings turned up for El Paso. The tool counts a repeat finding as the same standard recommendation appearing in more than one of your reports. Only grouped recommendations are compared, so a similar issue worded differently could be missed.

## 3. Problems the 2025 inspection noted but didn't turn into recommendations
Part of the report text was captured alongside your response to Rec 1. It lists problems OIG accepted as fixed by December 2025. Check that the fixes are still in place, because these are easy to slip back on:
- **Clean equipment stored in soiled utility rooms** (primary care and women's health). Separate rooms were designated and checked monthly. Is that still happening?
- **Expired respiratory masks** in a primary care storage room that the environment-of-care team hadn't inspected in six months because it was locked. Is the team actually getting into restricted rooms now?
- **Emergency alarm at an outpatient clinic** could only be reset from the police station. It was moved to a hallway nursing staff can reach. Is staff trained on resetting it?
- **Damaged concrete floor in a women's restroom**, a fall risk the network's FY2024 safety evaluation had also found. The captured text ends before saying whether it was fixed, so **confirm the repair yourself**.

## 4. Most common findings at other facilities (current inspection program, 112 reports)
These are ranked by how often they appear, not how serious they are, and they don't predict what OIG will find. El Paso has no recommendations in any of these groups, which doesn't prove you've never been cited for something similar.

**A. Communicating test results to providers and patients.** This is the biggest theme. It shows up in four groups covering 21, 12, 9 and 6 reports (some reports may be in more than one). Findings include:
- no written workflow for each service showing who does what (VHA Directive 1088(1))
- facility policy that doesn't meet VHA requirements
- no monitoring of whether patients were told about abnormal results

*What other facilities committed to:* service workflows on a standard template, reviewed by the Chief of Staff and Quality Management (Madison, 25-00254-277, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-william-s-middleton-memorial)); monthly random reviews of 50 test results reported to the Medical Executive Council until 90% compliance for six months (Hampton, 24-00603-86, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-hampton-healthcare-system)); 30 random charts a month per service chief (Walla Walla, 24-00599-202, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-jonathan-m-wainwright)).
**Check yourself:** Does every service that orders or reports tests have a current written workflow? Do you audit whether patients are notified, and do the results go to a committee?

**B. Cleanliness and safety in patient care areas** (11 and 9 reports). This matches your open Rec 1. Facilities committed to supervisor spot checks with numeric targets, such as 90% for six months and reports to the environment-of-care committee (Louisville, 24-03205-235, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare)), and an online channel for staff to report cleanliness problems (Salisbury, 26-00030-213, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-salisbury-va-health-care)).
**Check yourself:** Look under mattresses, exam table frames and sprinkler heads. Your Rec 1 plan doesn't yet name a compliance percentage or how long you'll track it, and other facilities' plans do.

**C. Stable leadership** (9 reports). These recommendations go to the VISN Director. If El Paso has many acting leaders, expect questions about it.

**D. Expired supplies and clean supply areas** (6 reports). This matches your expired-mask problem. Durham committed to weekly supply-room checks with sign-off sheets, plus 10 audits a month by the supply chief (24-00586-11, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-durham-va-health-care-system)). Watch the small storage spots outside the main supply rooms (Leeds, 24-00594-61, [link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-central-western)).

**Typical time to close:** about 140–256 days (median) for most of these groups. Some groups show a median of 0 days, but they have only 3–9 closed items each, and same-day closures pull the median down. Don't read 0 as typical.

## Caveats from the data
- Similar findings are grouped by wording and meaning. That points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one theme can split across several groups.
- Each target date is the facility's own estimate. They don't show whether a deadline was missed.
- A recommendation with no response in this data only means none was pulled from the report. It doesn't mean the facility didn't respond.

I can pull the full 2025 report with every recommendation and response, or search for more of what other facilities did on toxic exposure screening or test-result workflows.

**Why the data can't answer this:**
- **A target date is only the facility's own estimate** of when it will finish the work.
- **A closure date is probably when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence.** That can come months after the work was actually done.
- So a recommendation closed after its target date, or still open past it, doesn't show that VHA missed its commitment. It may only reflect when OIG finished its review.

**What the data does show for VHA (13,440 recommendations):**

| Measure | Value |

- **Closed the day the report came out:** 946 VHA recommendations were closed on the report's publication date, presumably because they were fixed beforehand. That pulls the median closure time down a little.
- **Shared recommendations:** A recommendation addressed to VHA and another office counts in both offices' totals.

**OIG doesn't name a "worst" VA medical center,** so I can't give you one from its records. OIG doesn't rank or grade facilities. This data source also deliberately avoids rating facilities, and its analysis tools can't group results by facility, so I can't build a league table either.

Simple rankings from OIG data would also be misleading:

- **Inspection timing varies.** Facilities are inspected on different cycles, so a facility inspected recently may show more open recommendations than one inspected years ago.
- **Report types differ.** A routine inspection, a hotline complaint review and a review after a specific incident produce very different numbers of findings. Many recommendations can come from one serious event or from a broad, thorough inspection.
- **Facility size and complexity vary.** A large tertiary-care hospital and a small rural center aren't comparable on raw counts.
- **Findings differ in weight.** One serious patient-safety finding can matter more than ten documentation findings.

**Here's what I can look up from OIG's public record:**

1. **One facility's history:** its reports, open recommendations, repeat findings and how its corrective actions were resolved.
2. **Problems that recur nationally:** which findings show up across many facilities and how long they usually take to close.
3. **Counts and trends** by year, VA office, topic or report type, such as how many recommendations are open or how long they take to close.
4. **Searching for specific issues,** such as suicide-prevention lapses, surgical events or staffing problems, with links to the reports.
5. **Comparing a few facilities you name,** side by side and with the caveats above.

If you have a particular facility or region in mind, or a specific concern like patient safety or wait times, tell me and I'll pull the records with report numbers and links.

**Nobody can say exactly what OIG will cite, and this data can't either.** OIG doesn't publish its inspection schedule or what it will find. Results depend on what inspectors see when they visit. What the public record can show is El Paso's own unresolved items and the findings that come up most often at other facilities. That's the best guide for preparing.

*Data as of 2026-11-04. It's current, not stale.*

## When the next inspection might happen (an estimate)
- **The last inspection ended 2025-01-16.** It was a Healthcare Facility Inspection, report **25-00193-155** ([link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system)), published 2026-07-16.
- **My estimate for the next one is around January 2028.** That's the last inspection's end date plus OIG's stated cycle of about three years. OIG publishes no schedule, so this is only an estimate.

## El Paso's 4 open recommendations: the clearest risks
Open items are the likeliest things for inspectors to check again.

**From report 25-00193-155** ([link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system)):
1. **Keeping the facility clean and safe** (environment of care). The facility's own target date is 2027-01-29. Its plan includes daily cleaning, restroom logs, 24 cleaning procedures, staff training completed June 2, 2026, and weekly rounds by the Associate Director. The same report also noted:
   - damaged concrete floor in a women's restroom, a fall risk that a regional (VISN) review had also flagged in FY 2024
   - clean and soiled items stored together, which the facility fixed, so no recommendation was made
   - expired respiratory masks in a storage room that review teams hadn't inspected in six months
2. **Completing secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days** (PACT Act). The target date is 2026-12-31. The facility reported zero screenings over 30 days as of June 2026. Its formal written procedure was still being drafted, and its goal is six months in a row at zero.

**From report 23-01179-204**, the 2023 information security inspection ([link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare)):

3. **A working, monitored video surveillance system for the data center** (assigned to VA's IT office).
4. **Water detection sensors in the data center** (also IT).

Both have been open since September 2023, and no response text is on file for either. That only means none was pulled from the report. It doesn't show that anything is overdue.

**Repeat findings: none.** Here that means the same standard recommendation hasn't shown up in more than one El Paso report. Only recommendations sorted into groups of similar findings are compared. Because OIG inspects against a standard checklist, a repeat would mean the issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.

## Most common findings at other facilities under the current program
These are sorted by how often they appear, not by severity. They are not predictions for El Paso.

| Finding theme | Share of reports |
|---|---|
| Written workflows for telling providers and patients about test results (VHA Directive 1088) | 21 of 112 |
| Test-result policy meets VHA rules, plus monitoring that patients are notified | 12 of 112 |
| Clean environment to reduce infection risk (VHA Directive 1608) | 11 of 112 |
| Regional (VISN) action for stable facility leadership | 9 of 112 |
| Patient care areas kept clean and safe | 9 of 112 |
| Test-result workflows for each service | 9 of 112 |
| No expired supplies, and clean supply areas | 6 of 112 |
| Monitoring whether providers tell patients about abnormal test results | 6 of 112 |

**Test-result communication is the most common theme by far.** It appears across several of these groups. None of El Paso's own recommendations fall into those groups, but that doesn't prove El Paso was never cited for something similar. It's worth checking against VHA Directive 1088 anyway. The cleanliness and expired-supply themes overlap directly with El Paso's open item #1.

Caveats from the data:
- Each group collects recommendations with similar wording. That suggests a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups.
- Some typical closure times rest on very small samples. Recommendations closed the day a report came out can pull them down to 0 days.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimates.

## Practical takeaways
1. Close out the cleanliness and toxic exposure screening items with documented evidence, such as audit results and months of sustained compliance.
2. Find out from the IT office where the data center camera and water sensor fixes stand. They've been open since 2023.
3. Do a self-check against the most common peer themes, especially test-result communication workflows and expired supplies.

I can pull other facilities' full corrective-action plans for any of these themes if you want to compare.
